catalog_quote: After a short preliminary study of the Nzima language it is only at present possible to record that "tone," or the pitch of the voice, is used to distinguish differences of meaning, and a full account of the extent to which this is the case, of the number of gradations of tone in use, and of the relation of the tones to vowel-length and stress, cannot as yet be given. Some notice, however, must be taken of tone from the very first, as there are words in common use in which an identical combination of consonant and vowel sounds is given a totally different meaning by the tone of the voice. PDF page 4 is book p. 74, headed "CHAPTER VI / TONES". new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule: Nzema is described as a tone language (pitch distinguishes word meaning; Welman marks acute for high and grave for low); the only mention of stress is that its relation to tone and vowel length had not yet been worked out. Modern phonology articles (Nyame 2025, 2026) mark high and low tones on Nzema words and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Welman gives a list of tonal minimal pairs (same segments, different meaning by tone) but no stress data.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (tonal minimal pairs, citation forms). No source opened makes any placement statement about word stress; this is a tonal-language description that is silent on stress placement, quoted because it explicitly names stress as undescribed.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe Nzema as spoken in Ghana (Welman 1925: Nzima of the Gold Coast, Axim/Jomoro area; Nyame 2025/2026: data from speakers at UEW/Ajumako, five dialects Dwɔmɔlɔ, Ɛlɛmgbɛlɛ, Ɛvaloɛ, Egila, Adwɔmɔlɔ). No dialect-specific claims about prosody. Berry 1955 (not opened) treats "the Nzema and Ahanta dialects" together (Ahanta = ahan1243).
